name: Hydrogen

bonding.summary: Two hydrogen atoms share one pair of electrons: the simplest covalent bond.
bonding.electronSharing: Each atom gives its single electron to the pair, so both feel two electrons, the full first shell like helium. The atoms are identical, so they share exactly equally.

formation: Formed as the early universe cooled: H + H- -> H2 + e-
occurrence: The most abundant molecule in the universe, filling giant molecular clouds where stars form.
facts: The H2 molecule is the most common molecule in the universe.
summary: Molecular hydrogen is two protons held together by one shared pair of electrons. It is the raw material from which stars form.

name: Helium hydride ion

bonding.summary: A helium atom and a proton share two electrons, both originally helium's.
bonding.electronSharing: Helium lends its two electrons to a bond with the bare proton. They stay much closer to helium, so the positive charge sits mostly on the hydrogen end.

formation: He + H+ -> HeH+ + light (radiative association, about 100,000 years after the Big Bang)
occurrence: Thought to be the first molecule ever formed; detected in space in 2019 in the planetary nebula NGC 7027.
uses: A test case for quantum-chemistry calculations
facts: It is the strongest known acid: it would protonate almost anything.
hazards: Exists only in space or in the lab as isolated ions.
summary: HeH+ is believed to be the very first molecule in the universe, formed when the first neutral helium atoms met free protons.

name: Trihydrogen cation

bonding.summary: Three protons share just two electrons in one bond that spans the whole triangle.
bonding.electronSharing: A single electron pair is spread over all three nuclei at once, the simplest example of a three-centre two-electron bond.

occurrence: One of the most abundant ions in interstellar space; also glows in Jupiter's and Saturn's auroras.
uses: Tracing the chemistry of interstellar clouds
facts: H3+ drives most of the chemistry in cold interstellar clouds by handing protons to other molecules.
hazards: Exists only in space or plasmas.
summary: H3+ is three protons bound by two shared electrons. It kick-starts the chemistry that builds molecules between the stars.

name: Carbon monoxide

bonding.summary: A triple bond: two pairs shared normally and a third pair donated by oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Carbon and oxygen share three electron pairs; one of them comes entirely from oxygen. Each atom keeps one lone pair. The dative pair nearly cancels oxygen's pull, so CO is only slightly polar.

formation: 2 C + O2 -> 2 CO (burning with too little oxygen)
occurrence: The second most common molecule in space after H2; on Earth from incomplete burning.
uses: Reducing iron ore in blast furnaces
Tracing star-forming gas in radio astronomy
facts: Astronomers map hydrogen clouds by the radio glow of the CO they contain.
hazards: Colorless, odorless and highly toxic: it binds to hemoglobin about 200 times more strongly than oxygen.
summary: Carbon monoxide has one of the strongest chemical bonds known. It is common in space and dangerous in homes.

name: Hydrogen cyanide

bonding.summary: A single H–C bond and a triple C≡N bond in a straight line.
bonding.electronSharing: Carbon shares one pair with hydrogen and three pairs with nitrogen. Nitrogen keeps one lone pair and pulls the shared electrons toward itself.

formation: CH4 + NH3 + 3/2 O2 -> HCN + 3 H2O (Andrussow process)
occurrence: Found in comets, interstellar clouds and Titan's atmosphere; made industrially.
facts: HCN can join with itself to form adenine, a building block of DNA, which is why it interests origin-of-life researchers.
summary: Hydrogen cyanide is a small, deadly molecule that is also a likely ingredient in the chemistry that led to life.

name: Formaldehyde

bonding.summary: Carbon bonds to two hydrogens and makes a double bond to oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: The C=O double bond shares two pairs, pulled strongly toward oxygen, which keeps two lone pairs.

formation: CH3OH -> CH2O + H2 (catalytic dehydrogenation of methanol)
occurrence: The first polyatomic organic molecule found in interstellar space (1969).
facts: Formalin, used to preserve specimens, is about 37% formaldehyde in water.
hazards: Toxic and a known human carcinogen.
summary: Formaldehyde is the simplest aldehyde. It is common in space and widely used to make resins.

name: Nitrogen

bonding.summary: A triple bond, one of the strongest bonds in chemistry (945 kJ/mol).
bonding.electronSharing: Each nitrogen shares three electrons, making three shared pairs, and keeps one lone pair.

formation: Separated from air by distilling liquid air
occurrence: 78% of Earth's atmosphere.
facts: Breaking the N≡N triple bond takes so much energy that the Haber process uses about 1% of the world's energy.
summary: N2's triple bond makes it so stable that most of the planet's nitrogen sits unused in the air.

name: Oxygen

bonding.summary: A double bond with two unpaired electrons.
bonding.electronSharing: In the simple picture the atoms share two pairs and each keeps two lone pairs. Molecular orbital theory shows two electrons are unpaired, which makes O2 magnetic and a 'diradical'.

formation: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2 (photosynthesis)
occurrence: 21% of the air, made by photosynthesis.
facts: Liquid oxygen sticks between the poles of a strong magnet.
summary: O2 is the oxygen we breathe. Its two unpaired electrons make it both reactive and magnetic.

name: Ozone

bonding.summary: Two equal O–O bonds, each halfway between single and double.
bonding.electronSharing: One pair of π electrons is spread over all three atoms (resonance). The central oxygen has a lone pair, which bends the molecule.

formation: 3 O2 -> 2 O3 (ultraviolet light or electric discharge)
occurrence: The ozone layer, 15–35 km up; also ground-level smog.
facts: The ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful UV-B and UV-C light.
summary: Ozone is a three-atom form of oxygen that shields life from ultraviolet light high in the sky but harms lungs near the ground.

name: Fluorine

bonding.summary: A single bond that is unusually weak (159 kJ/mol).
bonding.electronSharing: The atoms share one pair; each keeps three lone pairs that repel each other across the short bond, weakening it.

formation: 2 HF -> H2 + F2 (electrolysis of KF in liquid HF)
occurrence: Never free in nature; made by electrolysis.
facts: The weak F–F bond plus very strong bonds to other elements make fluorine the most reactive element.
summary: F2 is the most reactive element in molecular form, held together by a surprisingly weak bond.

name: Chlorine

bonding.summary: One shared pair links two chlorine atoms.
bonding.electronSharing: Each atom contributes one electron to the pair and keeps three lone pairs, completing its octet.

formation: 2 NaCl + 2 H2O -> Cl2 + H2 + 2 NaOH (chlor-alkali electrolysis)
occurrence: Made from salt water.
facts: About 70 million tonnes of chlorine are produced each year.
summary: Chlorine gas is made from salt water and used to disinfect water worldwide.

name: Bromine

bonding.summary: A single shared pair; strong attraction between large molecules makes it liquid.
bonding.electronSharing: One shared pair and three lone pairs on each atom. The big, soft electron clouds attract neighboring molecules.

formation: 2 Br- + Cl2 -> Br2 + 2 Cl- (from brines)
occurrence: Extracted from brine wells and the Dead Sea.
facts: One of only two elements liquid at room temperature.
summary: Bromine is a dense red-brown liquid made of Br2 molecules.

name: Iodine

bonding.summary: A long single bond; stronger attraction between molecules makes iodine a solid.
bonding.electronSharing: One shared pair, three lone pairs on each atom.

formation: 2 I- + Cl2 -> I2 + 2 Cl- (from brines and seaweed)
occurrence: From brines, Chilean saltpeter deposits and seaweed.
facts: Iodine vapor is violet; dissolved in water with iodide it is brown.
summary: Iodine forms shiny dark crystals that turn straight into violet vapor.

name: White phosphorus

bonding.summary: Six P–P single bonds along the edges of a tetrahedron.
bonding.electronSharing: Each phosphorus shares one pair with each of the other three atoms and keeps one lone pair. The 60° angles strain the bonds.

formation: 2 Ca3(PO4)2 + 6 SiO2 + 10 C -> P4 + 6 CaSiO3 + 10 CO
occurrence: Made from phosphate rock in electric furnaces.
facts: White phosphorus glows in the dark as it slowly reacts with air (chemiluminescence).
hazards: Highly toxic; ignites spontaneously in air.
summary: P4 is a tiny, strained tetrahedron of phosphorus atoms, which makes it dangerously reactive.

name: Cyclooctasulfur

bonding.summary: Eight sulfur atoms in a puckered crown-shaped ring.
bonding.electronSharing: Each sulfur shares one pair with each ring neighbor and keeps two lone pairs.

formation: Recovered as H2S from natural gas: 2 H2S + O2 -> 2 S + 2 H2O (Claus process; S8 rings form on cooling)
occurrence: Volcanic deposits; most is recovered from natural gas and oil.
facts: Above about 160 °C the rings break open and link into long chains, so molten sulfur suddenly becomes thick.
hazards: Low toxicity; burns to toxic SO2.
summary: Ordinary yellow sulfur is a crystal of S8 crown-shaped rings.

name: Buckminsterfullerene

bonding.summary: 60 carbons each bonded to three others; 30 double bonds lie on the edges shared by two hexagons.
bonding.electronSharing: Each carbon shares pairs with three neighbors and contributes one electron to π bonding spread over the cage.

formation: Carbon vaporized by a laser or electric arc in helium condenses into C60 cages
occurrence: Found in soot, some rocks, and in space around dying stars.
facts: Its discovery in 1985 earned Kroto, Curl and Smalley the 1996 Nobel Prize.
C60 was detected in a planetary nebula in 2010; it sublimes rather than melting.
summary: C60 is a hollow sphere of carbon shaped exactly like a football, a third form of pure carbon after graphite and diamond.

name: Carbon dioxide

bonding.summary: Two C=O double bonds pointing in opposite directions.
bonding.electronSharing: Carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen; oxygen pulls them closer (Δχ 0.89). Each oxygen keeps two lone pairs. The two bond dipoles cancel, so CO2 is nonpolar overall.

formation: C + O2 -> CO2; CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O (burning)
occurrence: About 0.042% of air (420 ppm in 2024) and rising.
facts: Solid CO2 sublimes at −78.5 °C at normal pressure; it is liquid only above 5.1 atm.
hazards: Asphyxiant at high concentration; main driver of climate change.
summary: CO2 is what plants breathe in and what burning releases. It traps heat in the atmosphere.

name: Nitrous oxide

bonding.summary: N–N–O in a line, with bonding between the N≡N–O and N=N=O pictures.
bonding.electronSharing: Resonance spreads the bonding pairs so the N–N bond is about 2.5 and the N–O bond about 1.5. The central nitrogen carries a partial positive charge.

formation: NH4NO3 -> N2O + 2 H2O (heating ammonium nitrate)
occurrence: Made by soil bacteria and fertilized fields; about 0.34 ppm in air.
facts: N2O is the largest remaining ozone-depleting emission and a potent greenhouse gas.
hazards: Asphyxiant; misuse damages nerves via vitamin B12.
summary: Laughing gas is a mild anesthetic and an important greenhouse gas.

name: Nitric oxide

bonding.summary: Bond order 2.5 with one unpaired electron: a stable radical.
bonding.electronSharing: NO has 11 valence electrons, so one is left unpaired. It sits mostly on nitrogen and makes NO reactive.

formation: N2 + O2 -> 2 NO (lightning and hot engines)
occurrence: From lightning, combustion and living cells.
uses: Medical gas for lung blood vessels
facts: The discovery that NO is a signal molecule in the body won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Medicine.
summary: NO is a tiny radical that pollutes city air yet also signals blood vessels to relax.

name: Nitrogen dioxide

bonding.summary: Two equal N–O bonds of order 1.5 and one unpaired electron.
bonding.electronSharing: Resonance spreads one π pair over both N–O bonds. The single unpaired electron on nitrogen bends the molecule less than a lone pair would.

formation: 2 NO + O2 -> 2 NO2
occurrence: The brown haze of urban smog.
facts: Two NO2 molecules pair their lone electrons to form colorless N2O4 when cooled.
hazards: Toxic; irritates lungs and forms acid rain.
summary: NO2 is the reddish-brown gas of smog.

name: Sulfur dioxide

bonding.summary: Two strong S–O bonds and a lone pair on sulfur.
bonding.electronSharing: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself. The lone pair on sulfur bends the molecule, so SO2 is polar.

formation: S + O2 -> SO2
occurrence: Volcanoes and burning sulfur-containing coal and oil.
facts: Large volcanic eruptions can cool the planet by forming sulfate haze from SO2.
summary: SO2 has a sharp smell of burnt matches and is the main cause of acid rain.

name: Sulfur trioxide

bonding.summary: Three equivalent S–O bonds in a flat triangle; no lone pair on sulfur.
bonding.electronSharing: Sulfur's six valence electrons all bond to oxygen; the strongly polar bonds cancel by symmetry.

formation: 2 SO2 + O2 -> 2 SO3 (vanadium pentoxide catalyst, contact process)
occurrence: Made industrially; forms in polluted air.
facts: SO3 reacts with water so violently that it is absorbed into sulfuric acid instead.
summary: SO3 is the key intermediate in making sulfuric acid.

name: Dichlorodifluoromethane (Freon-12)

bonding.summary: Carbon bonds to two chlorines and two fluorines in a tetrahedron.
bonding.electronSharing: Fluorine and chlorine both pull shared electrons away from carbon. UV light high in the atmosphere breaks the weaker C–Cl bonds, releasing chlorine atoms.

formation: CCl4 + 2 HF -> CCl2F2 + 2 HCl
occurrence: Synthetic; banned by the 1987 Montreal Protocol.
uses: Formerly refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol cans
facts: One chlorine atom from a CFC can destroy thousands of ozone molecules.
hazards: Ozone-depleting and a powerful greenhouse gas.
summary: CFC-12 was the miracle refrigerant that turned out to tear a hole in the ozone layer.
